2.1.stem: Which of the following statements about Maxwell's equations and the derived EM wave equation are correct? (Select all that apply)
options: Maxwell's equations in vacuum are Gauss's law, Gauss's law for magnetism, the Maxwell–Faraday equation, and Ampère's circuital law
The wave equation ∇²E = μ0ε0 ∂²E/∂t² can be derived starting from Maxwell's equations
A time-harmonic field oscillating at a single frequency is called monochromatic
The wavevector amplitude k relates to wavelength via k = λ/2π
Visible light corresponds to wavelengths outside the 390–780 nm range
2.1.explanation: Maxwell's four vacuum equations, the derived wave equation, and the definition of a monochromatic time-harmonic field are all stated directly in the notes. k = 2π/λ (not λ/2π), and visible light is defined as λ ∈ 390–780 nm, not outside it.

2.2.stem: Which of the following are true about the behavior of light at an interface between two media, according to geometrical optics? (Select all that apply)
options: Part of the incident ray reflects and part refracts
The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (θi = θr)
Snell's law relates the angles via ni sinθi = nt sinθt
Reflection and refraction occur in two unrelated, non-coplanar planes
In a homogeneous medium, rays propagate along curved paths
2.2.explanation: The notes state that part of a ray reflects and part refracts, with θi=θr and Snell's law ni sinθi = nt sinθt, all within the same plane of incidence. Rays propagate straight (not curved) in a homogeneous medium.

3.2.stem: Which of the following are correct properties of the 1D wave equation ∂²ψ/∂z² = (1/v²)∂²ψ/∂t², derived for ψ(z,t) = f(z ± vt)? (Select all that apply)
options: The wave function ψ must be differentiable at least twice
The equation is obtained by differentiating ψ with respect to both z and t and combining the results
The equation's form still depends on an arbitrary choice of coordinate orientation
v is the propagation velocity of the wave
The equation only describes waves travelling in the +z direction
3.2.explanation: The notes derive the equation by twice-differentiating ψ=f(z±vt) and require it to be twice differentiable; v is the propagation speed. The whole point of moving to the second-order equation was to remove direction-dependence, and ±vt covers both +z and −z propagation.

3.7.stem: For a 3D plane wave ψ(r,t) = A e^{i(k·r − ωt)}, which of the following statements are correct? (Select all that apply)
options: The wavevector k defines the wave's propagation direction
The phasefront is the surface on which the phase is constant
The phase velocity is vp = ω/k
The phase must depend quadratically on position r
k·r is constant everywhere on a plane perpendicular to k
3.7.explanation: The notes require the phase to depend linearly (not quadratically) on r, define the phasefront as the constant-phase plane perpendicular to k, and derive vp=ω/k from the total differential of the phase.

4.1.stem: Which of the following are correct statements about the vacuum Maxwell's equations and the derived EM wave equation? (Select all that apply)
options: In vacuum, ρ = 0 and J = 0 are assumed
Both E and B satisfy the same form of wave equation
The speed of light is c0 = 1/√(μ0ε0)
c0 depends on the refractive index of the surrounding medium
The wave equation for B is derived by taking the curl of Ampère's law and applying Lagrange's vector identity
4.1.explanation: ρ=0, J=0 in vacuum; both ∇²E and ∇²B reduce to the same wave equation with speed c0=1/√(μ0ε0), derived via the curl and Lagrange's formula. c0 is a vacuum constant of nature, independent of any medium.

5.3.stem: Which of the following are true about the Lorentz model of an atom? (Select all that apply)
options: The electron is modeled as attached to the atomic core via a harmonic spring
The model works particularly well for dielectric materials
The model works well for metals
The resonance frequency is ω0 = (k/m)^(1/2)
The imaginary part of the derived refractive index corresponds to absorption
5.3.explanation: The notes describe the harmonic-spring electron model, its resonance frequency ω0=(k/m)^(1/2), its good fit for dielectrics, and that Im(n) corresponds to absorption. The model works poorly for metals (the Drude model is used there instead).

6.6.stem: Which of the following are true about total internal reflection (TIR)? (Select all that apply)
options: TIR can occur when light travels from an optically denser medium toward a less dense one, beyond the critical angle
The critical angle satisfies sinθc = nt/ni
The Fresnel transmission coefficients become exactly zero during TIR
An evanescent field exists just beyond the interface during TIR, decaying exponentially away from it
TIR is used in optical fibers, waveguides, and reflecting prisms
6.6.explanation: TIR occurs beyond the critical angle sinθc=nt/ni when going from a denser to a less dense medium; the notes explicitly state TIR does NOT mean the transmission coefficients vanish — an exponentially evanescent surface field forms instead. TIR is used in fibers, waveguides, prisms, and Fresnel rhombs.

7.3.stem: A wave reflects perfectly off a mirror at z=0, forming a standing wave. Which of the following are correct? (Select all that apply)
options: The total field does not propagate
Nodes are locations where the field amplitude is always zero
Antinodes are locations of maximum field amplitude
For a perfect mirror, the reflected amplitude equals the incident amplitude with the same sign (AR = AI)
The standing wave still oscillates harmonically in time
7.3.explanation: The notes describe a non-propagating field with nodes (zero amplitude) and antinodes (maximum amplitude), oscillating harmonically in time. The perfect-mirror boundary condition gives AR = −AI, not AR = AI.

7.5.stem: Which of the following are true about optical coherence? (Select all that apply)
options: A perfectly time-harmonic monochromatic wave is fully coherent but not physically realistic
Coherence time τc is the time interval within which the phase stays correlated
Coherence distance is ℓc = τc · c
Coherence is strictly a binary (all-or-nothing) property of real light sources
Real light can be modeled as separate wave packets that are internally coherent but not mutually coherent
7.5.explanation: The notes describe the idealized fully-coherent monochromatic wave, coherence time/distance (ℓc=τc·c), and the wave-packet model. They explicitly note coherence vanishes gradually rather than being a strict binary property.

8.4.stem: Which of the following are true about the Michelson interferometer? (Select all that apply)
options: It consists of a 50/50 beamsplitter, two mirrors, and a detector
The optical path difference is Λ = 2(d2 − d1)
For a broadband source, the interferogram (minus its constant term) is related to the source's spectrum via a Fourier cosine transform
Only strictly monochromatic sources can be used with a Michelson interferometer
A camera can be used as the detector when light arrives off the optical axis
8.4.explanation: The notes describe the beamsplitter/mirrors/detector layout, path difference Λ=2d, the Fourier-transform relation used for spectrometry, and camera detection at an angle θ (replacing d with d·cosθ). Broadband sources are explicitly handled too, not just monochromatic ones.

9.2.stem: Which of the following are true about Fraunhofer diffraction? (Select all that apply)
options: It applies in the far field, when R > a²/λ
The diffracted field is approximately proportional to the 2D Fourier transform of the aperture field
It requires the observation point to be very close to the aperture
A lens can be used to image the diffraction pattern
The quadratic phase term becomes significant (not negligible) in the Fraunhofer regime
9.2.explanation: The Fraunhofer condition R>a²/λ is a far-field (not near-field) condition, under which the quadratic phase term is negligible and the resulting field is the 2D Fourier transform of the aperture field; a lens can be used to image the resulting pattern.

9.5.stem: Which of the following are true about diffraction gratings? (Select all that apply)
options: A diffraction maximum forms when the phase difference between waves from adjacent slits equals 2πm
The grating equation is a(sinθm − sinθi) = mλ
Blazed gratings can enhance or suppress specific diffraction orders
Diffraction gratings can only operate in transmission, never in reflection
The mth diffraction maximum is called the mth diffraction order
9.5.explanation: The notes give the grating equation a(sinθm−sinθi)=mλ from the 2πm phase condition, define the mth maximum as the mth order, and mention blazed gratings for order-shaping. Gratings can operate in either transmission or reflection.

10.3.stem: Which of the following are true about thin lenses? (Select all that apply)
options: For a thin lens in air, the lensmaker's equation is 1/f = (nℓ/nm − 1)(1/R1 − 1/R2)
Convex lenses have f > 0
Concave lenses have f > 0
The Gaussian thin-lens equation is 1/so + 1/si = 1/f
Lens power D is defined as D = f (the focal length itself)
10.3.explanation: The notes give the lensmaker's equation, the sign convention f>0 for convex lenses (f<0 for concave), and the Gaussian thin-lens form 1/so+1/si=1/f. Lens power is defined as D ≡ 1/f, not D=f.

10.13.stem: Which of the following are true about simple two-lens telescopes? (Select all that apply)
options: The telescope's angular magnification is MT = fo/fe
A Keplerian telescope produces an inverted image
A Galilean telescope uses a negative eyepiece focal length and produces an upright image
Both the Galilean and Keplerian designs are completely free of chromatic aberration
The Newtonian telescope reduces chromatic aberration by replacing the objective lens with a mirror
10.13.explanation: MT=fo/fe is the telescope magnification; Keplerian designs (fe>0) invert the image while Galilean designs (fe<0) keep it upright. Both lens-based designs are susceptible to chromatic aberration, which the mirror-based Newtonian design largely avoids.
